title: Bitline charge recycling between paired subarrays during refresh
idea: Ideal: refresh costs zero energy. Closest: at the end of each refresh, the high bitlines of one subarray dump half their charge through a 180 nm transfer switch into the bitlines of the next subarray to be refreshed, so each refresh reuses roughly half of the previous one's CV2.
why: Facts 3 and 10: refresh energy ~-40% without lowering the voltage floor.

title: eDRAM's refresh burden replaced by decay-as-miss caches
idea: Intel's Crystal Well and IBM POWER eDRAM caches were dropped partly over refresh power and hot retention. Fix: never refresh; each line carries a coarse write-epoch tag, any line older than its retention budget or failing ECC is treated as a cache miss and refetched, and dirty lines are evicted before their epoch expires.
why: Zero refresh power; the retention tail becomes a slight miss-rate increase, so dense eDRAM or stacked-DRAM cache dies can use leaky, cheap cells (fact 3).

title: Spare hybrid-bond pads with bit-steering for plasma-activated bonding
idea: Rearrange the bond interface into a repairable bus: HF-free surface prep (N2/O2 plasma activation, water rinse) leaves more bond voids, so each 32-pad group carries 2 spare pads and a bit-steering mux, configured at stack test, that routes around open pads.
why: Keeps hybrid-bonded DRAM stack yield above ~99% despite higher void density, cheaper than TSV-stack yield loss.

title: Per-row polarity flag parks most cells in hammer-immune state
idea: Worse: store data so the maximum number of cells sit in the charged state that hammer-induced leakage attacks. Flip: add one flag bit per 64B chunk and write the data or its inverse, whichever leaves more cells in the discharged orientation for their true/anti-cell type, so most victim cells have no charge to lose.
why: Fact 9: hammer flips are strongly directional; halving the average number of charged cells roughly halves flippable bits per victim row and also lowers retention-failure exposure, for ~0.2% capacity.

title: Bistable NEMS beam tier quarantines hammer-hot rows
idea: Box [medium: bistable buckled nanobeam | access: electrostatic actuation | sense: capacitive position | integration: BEOL MEMS above array | substrate: bulk | fab: sacrificial-release MEMS]. A small on-die tier of mechanically latched cells, which hold no disturbable charge and do not leak, receives rows the controller flags as hammered or leaky until they cool.
why: Facts 9/3: physically immune cells absorb the worst ~0.1% of rows, removing most mitigation refreshes.

title: Aviation dissimilar redundancy: cross-vendor ECC words
idea: Adapted from fly-by-wire systems that use dissimilar processors from different vendors so one design flaw cannot fail every channel: each ECC codeword in a module or CXL pool is assembled from dies of at least three different vendors or process lots, so a vendor-specific weakness (a hammer-sensitive layout, a lot-wide retention excursion) can hit only one symbol.
why: Row hammer and correlated failures (facts 3, 9): chipkill assumes independent dies, but real failures cluster by vendor and lot; dissimilar assembly makes existing ECC far stronger in practice and lets riskier lower-bin parts fill each slot.

title: Thin-film Peltier strips cool only refresh-dominant hot banks
idea: Effect: Peltier thermoelectric cooling. A Bi2Te3/Sb2Te3 superlattice thin-film cooler in the interposer under the HBM base die pumps heat out of the 2-4 banks sitting over GPU hotspots, dropping them ~10 C; the controller runs it only when the computed refresh-energy saving exceeds the Peltier power.
why: High-temperature refresh: leakage halves per ~10 C, so hot banks avoid the 2x refresh mode above 85 C, and the row-hammer threshold also improves at lower temperature.

title: Si: retention-graded silicon sells dies failing 64 ms as R-grade
idea: Create a JEDEC-style relaxed-retention grade (e.g., 16 ms refresh window) with a per-die weak-row map written into SPD; host controllers refresh faster only where flagged, and AI-inference fleets buy these dies at a discount.
why: Recovers dies now scrapped or down-binned for retention tails (est. 3-8% of output), raising usable supply during the 4x price spike.

title: Write data so weak cells hold their leak-to value
idea: Inverts 'data is stored as-is': each 64-bit word carries 2 coset bits selecting one of four XOR masks; the write encoder picks the mask that leaves the word's known weak cells (true-cells leak to 0, anti-cells to 1) already in their discharged state, so leakage cannot corrupt them.
why: Neutralizes most retention-tail cells (fact 3) for 3% overhead; with 1-2 weak cells per word the refresh interval can rise ~4-8x.

title: Errors as cache misses: detect-only DRAM refetches peer replica
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: for read-only AI weights replicated across a cluster, U.S.-made inference memory carries only a cheap CRC per 4 KB page; a detected error discards the page and refetches it from a peer node's copy over the fabric, so cells may run at raw BER ~1e-5.
why: Drops on-die ECC and most guardbands for this tier: ~6% parity reclaimed, refresh stretched ~10x and weak dies usable, at negligible refetch traffic.

title: Bit-plane-transposed tensors: exponent planes refreshed, mantissa planes left drifting
idea: Combine approximate computing with bit-plane storage: the controller transposes BF16/FP8 tensors so each DRAM row holds one bit-plane; sign/exponent planes go to normally refreshed rows and low-mantissa planes to rows refreshed 8-16x less often, so any flip lands at a known, low significance.
why: Refresh cost (fact 3): AI tensors fill most HBM; cutting refresh on ~50-60% of bits saves ~5-10% DRAM power/bandwidth and lets weak-retention dies be sold into AI.

title: Nanoimprint template defects become one shared repair map
idea: No EUV: nanoimprint lithography copies identical template defects onto every die at the same coordinates. Time/scale shift (one template -> millions of dies over its life): characterize the template once and pre-fuse one universal repair map into every die it prints, adding to the map only when the template degrades.
why: Removes most per-die repair test time and lets cheap NIL replace EUV for critical array layers despite its higher defect rate.

title: Self-assembled block-copolymer capacitor holes replace EUV layers
idea: Po: chips grown, not made. Capacitor hole arrays are patterned by directed self-assembly of a cylinder-forming block copolymer guided by a coarse DUV template; DSA's ~0.1-1% missing or merged holes, which kept it out of production, become dead cells that the code treats as erasures.
why: Capital/EUV (fact 4): removes 1-2 EUV layers (~5-10% wafer cost) while reaching ~10 nm-class hole pitch by self-assembly.

title: Registration-mark pilot cells recalibrate sense references for every row
idea: Like the registration marks that align a press's colour plates, write 2-4 known pilot cells (one charged, one discharged) into each row at every restore; on activation a small comparator measures the pilot bitline swings and shifts that row's sense-amp reference and sensing delay on the fly, so rows whose cells have drifted (leakage, temperature, ageing) still sense correctly.
why: Turns marginal retention-tail reads into recoverable margin, allowing ~2-4x longer refresh or cells with ~30% less Cs (facts 1, 3) for ~0.5% cell overhead.

title: Homeostatic plasticity: sense reference self-trims to keep 50% ones
idea: Neurons scale their synapses to hold average firing constant; because bus data is scrambled, each mat's reads should average ~50% ones, so a per-mat counter tracks the running ones-fraction and nudges the sense reference/precharge level to restore balance, cancelling temperature, aging and leakage drift before it becomes errors.
why: Voltage floor (VARY ~1 V) and retention tail: recovers ~10-20% of signal margin otherwise spent as guard-band, enabling lower array voltage or smaller Cs.

title: $1-IoT repairless DRAM: no fuses, no spares, a bad-row map
idea: Ultra-cheap IoT parts cannot afford repair. Remove laser and e-fuse repair, spare rows and columns, and the repair test insertion from the die. Instead, store the bad-row list measured at test in a tiny OTP block that the host reads at boot, and map around those rows in page tables.
why: Repair circuitry, fuses and repair test cost periphery area (fact 7: periphery is ~49%) and tester time. That saves ~3-5% die area and one test step per die, with the OS managing the holes.

title: Interposer ECC chiplet serves array-only DUV memory dies
idea: No EUV: strip ECC, repair logic and most periphery from the DUV memory die and put them on one mature-node logic chiplet on a silicon interposer that serves 8 array dies. The chiplet can run long codes across all of them.
why: Shrinks the ~49% periphery share on each DUV array die and pools reliability logic across dies at package scale.

title: F: fluorine-hardened recess-gate edge resists hot-carrier depassivation
idea: A tilted low-dose fluorine implant aimed only at the gate-to-storage-node overlap corner replaces Si-H with Si-F bonds (~5.7 eV vs ~3.1 eV), so hammer-induced hot carriers and GIDL fields cannot re-create the interface traps behind RTN and variable retention time.
why: Cuts VRT cells and lifetime growth of the leakage tail (fact 3) plus trap-assisted hammer coupling (fact 9); target ~2x fewer VRT cells.

title: Substitute static ferroelectric storage with rolling polarity rotation against imprint
idea: Store data XOR a per-region epoch mask and rewrite regions in background with the mask flipped on a slow schedule, tracked by an epoch bit, so no ferroelectric capacitor sits in one polarization long enough to imprint.
why: Imprint/retention failure is a key HZO FeRAM reliability limiter; rotation keeps switching windows symmetric for years at ~1% bandwidth.

title: Natick-style fail-in-place pods: sealed nitrogen memory sleds, never serviced
idea: Microsoft's sealed undersea datacenter had one-eighth the server failure rate of a land control group and was never touched by technicians. Build sealed, dry-nitrogen DDR5 memory sleds overprovisioned by 15% with rank sparing. The controller retires failing DIMMs in place, and the sled is swapped only at 5-year end of life.
why: Eliminates service labor and lets operators deploy lower-bin DIMMs, because spares absorb their failures. That cuts cost per usable bit by ~5-10% at fleet scale.

title: Coulomb-blockade nanodot node suppresses leakage by charging energy
idea: A ~2 nm Si nanodot has C ~0.2 aF, so the single-electron charging energy e^2/2C ~0.4 eV ~15 kT, and every escape is penalized by ~exp(-15) on top of the tunnel barrier. Store a bit as N vs N+k electrons, sense with an SET-like gain stage, and vote across 3 dots per bit.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) and density: ~1e6x leakage suppression in principle, with no capacitor at all.

title: Williams-tube interlaced raster: rotating row interlace starves row hammer
idea: Williams-tube memories limited the 'read-around ratio' (charge spill from reading neighbouring spots) by interlacing the raster so neighbours were regenerated before spill accumulated. Logical rows map to physical rows through an interlace whose stride and phase rotate every 1/16 of the refresh window, and the migration piggybacks on refresh (each refresh reads a row and writes it into its new slot), so no aggressor keeps the same physical victims long enough to reach ~1k activations.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): disturb per victim is capped per phase instead of per window, ~16x margin with no per-row counters; periphery cost is one address-permutation unit per bank.

title: Capsid proofreading: reversible self-assembly anneals out patterning defects
idea: Virus capsids assemble from weakly bonded subunits that unbind and rebind, so misassembled pieces fall off; pattern cell arrays with block-copolymer or DNA-tile self-assembly using cyclic annealing at temperatures where misplaced domains dissolve and correct ones persist, driving defect density to memory grade without EUV.
why: EUV capital (5-7 layers, ~55% depreciation): self-assembled 10-15 nm patterns at near-zero tool cost, with the classic DSA defect blocker fixed by thermodynamic proofreading; key route to ~100x cheaper patterning per bit.

title: CDMA code-division storage across simultaneously activated rows
idea: Adapted from CDMA cellular radio, where users share a channel through orthogonal spreading codes and despreading averages out noise: k data bits are stored across N cells on one bitline with Walsh-coded charge levels written by N simultaneously activated wordlines; on read the same multi-row activation sums charge on the bitline and a code-matched sense sequence recovers each bit with processing gain, so any single leaky or dead cell only adds noise.
why: Capacitor wall and retention tail (facts 1, 3): processing gain of ~10log(N/k) dB lets individual cells shrink to ~1-2 fF and makes isolated leaky cells irrelevant, removing most row/column repair and relaxing refresh.

title: Proof-of-work logic: speculative-decoding drafts run from junk DRAM
idea: Crypto miners shrug off memory errors because every result is cheaply verified. Host LLM speculative-decoding draft models and their caches on retention-reject or relaxed-refresh DIMMs: the full model's verification pass rejects any token a memory error corrupted, so the only cost is a slightly lower acceptance rate.
why: Creates a productive market for weak-bin DRAM (several percent of output) and frees premium HBM for the target model (fact 3).

title: Co-aged reference cells cancel drift in printed ionic memory
idea: Box [medium: proton-intercalation WO3 ionic cell | access: printed organic diode | sense: ratiometric current | integration: 3D printed tiers | substrate: polymer foil | fab: inkjet printing]. Every row write also writes four reference cells to known levels at the same instant so they age identically; reads compare each data cell against interpolated co-aged references, cancelling time and temperature drift.
why: Capital and scarce resources: makes very cheap, drift-prone printed media usable as working memory; drift-induced errors suppressed ~100x.

title: Miura-ori keyed fold scrambles physical row adjacency every boot
idea: A Miura-ori fold sends sheet neighbours far apart; add a tiny programmable mapping layer in each subarray's row decoder that applies a per-boot secret keyed permutation, so logically adjacent rows are physically distant and an attacker cannot tell which rows sandwich a victim; correlated physical faults are also spread across codewords.
why: Targeted double-sided hammering (fact 9) needs adjacency knowledge; a keyed fold makes it probabilistically infeasible without per-row counters.

title: Toshiba's forgotten 4-level DRAM, Gray-mapped like Frank Gray's tube
idea: Toshiba (1989) and NEC (1996) demonstrated 2-bit/cell DRAM and then dropped it; Frank Gray's 1947 PCM coding tube used reflected-binary code so a beam landing between zones made only a one-bit error. Store 2 bits per cell as four charge levels with Gray mapping, read by a two-step charge-sharing sense amp, so leakage drift into the adjacent level costs one bit, which a light per-word BCH repairs.
why: Density and cost per bit (fact 4): ~1.8x bits per area without a litho node; Gray mapping converts the dominant MLC failure (one-level drift) into single-bit errors; needs ~2x refresh and much tighter sensing.

title: Safety-stock ECC: spare parity chips loaned as capacity while healthy
idea: Inventory systems size safety stock to demand variance. On 10-chip DDR5 ECC DIMMs, the FPGA/CXL controller packs data into the two ECC chips for regions with a measured-low error rate, protecting them with a small CRC carved from the data. When telemetry shows errors rising, the region converts back to full ECC and the OS gives the capacity back.
why: Adds up to +25% usable capacity from existing DIMMs in healthy regions during the shortage, while weak regions keep full protection.

title: Theatre understudy: on-module spare die shadows the riskiest die
idea: Adapted from theatre understudies who rehearse the lead's part so the show goes on: an RDIMM carries one extra die whose data path is steered by a trailing-node mux; firmware watches per-die correctable-error trends and continuously mirrors whichever die is degrading fastest into the understudy, swapping it out with no data loss when it crosses a threshold.
why: Field failure and screening cost: modules can be built from lower-bin dies because the single most likely failure is pre-mirrored; one spare per 10 dies (~10% capacity) can replace stricter and costlier screening.

title: No tracking state: keyed rotating row permutation defeats hammering
idea: Imposed limit: no per-row tracking state. Each refresh window, the bank rekeys a lightweight Feistel permutation that maps logical to physical rows within a subarray, migrating a few rows per refresh command. An attacker cannot keep hammering the same physical neighbors long enough to cause a flip.
why: Fact 9: probabilistic hammer immunity at near-zero area; cost is ~1-2% extra row copies during refresh.

title: Z-RAM refresh eliminated by buried-well BJT feedback bistable bodies
idea: Z-RAM failed partly because floating-body charge leaked out in milliseconds and needed refresh. Fix: add a buried n-well beneath each floating body so the parasitic vertical BJT continuously replenishes holes by impact ionization when the body is charged and stays off when empty (Zeno-style bistable floating body), latching both states statically.
why: Zero refresh power: the latch self-restores, so disturb- or alpha-induced charge loss heals automatically; a capacitor-free 1T cell attacks facts 1, 3 and 9, provided holding current stays in the pA range.

title: Building expansion joints: compliant spring microbumps for HBM stacks
idea: Adapted from expansion joints that let bridges and buildings move with temperature without cracking: replace rigid microbumps in HBM stacks with helical or serpentine copper micro-springs electroplated in a sacrificial resist mold, absorbing CTE mismatch and warpage during bonding and thermal cycling so TSVs and bumps do not crack.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): much of the 20-30% stack yield loss and early-life failure comes from bonding stress and warpage; compliant joints could recover ~5-10 points of stack yield and allow thinner dies.

title: Z-channel asymmetric code with minority-charge data inversion
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: retention failures are almost only charged-to-discharged, so each word stores an inversion flag that minimizes charged cells (using the known true/anti-cell polarity of each row) and is protected by a Z-channel asymmetric code that corrects only charge-loss flips.
why: Asymmetric codes need ~30-40% fewer check bits for equal correction, and at most half the cells are ever charged, halving leakage exposure; relaxes the retention-tail spec ~2-4x.

title: Display mura compensation for sense-amp offset to shrink periphery
idea: Adapted from OLED/LCD panels, which measure per-region non-uniformity at the factory and apply stored correction constants at runtime: each sense amp's offset is measured at test or boot and stored as a 3-bit trim in a dense one-time-programmable array, which injects a small compensating charge before sensing so sense-amp transistors can be drawn at minimum size.
why: Periphery at ~49% of die (fact 7): sense amps oversized for mismatch are a big periphery block; offset trimming could shrink them ~30-40%, cutting die area ~5-8% while keeping read margin for weaker cells.

title: Curie-tuned barium strontium titanate gains capacitance as it heats
idea: Worse: use dielectrics whose capacitance stays flat while leakage doubles every 10 C, so hot chips lose data fastest. Flip: tune the Ba/Sr ratio of a (Ba,Sr)TiO3 capacitor so its permittivity peak sits near 85-95 C; as the die heats, Cs rises and partly offsets the faster leakage, flattening retention versus temperature.
why: Fact 3: hot-case refresh sets the spec; temperature-compensated Cs could cut worst-case refresh rate ~2x using Ba, Sr, Ti and O instead of Hf.

title: Hippocampal CA3 attractors: noisy printed crossbars that self-correct on recall
idea: CA3 recurrent networks recall whole memories from noisy cues; store data as attractors of a dense associative (modern Hopfield) network whose weights sit in a printed resistive crossbar with +-30% variation and dead devices, so iterating recall pulls errors back to the stored pattern and the array itself acts as the decoder.
why: Cost per GB: tolerates device variation that makes conventional cells useless, admitting printed/roll-to-roll media at a tiny fraction of wafer cost; trades multi-iteration latency (~us) and 3-10x capacity overhead.

title: Von Neumann multiplexed bundles make defect-ridden 3D DRAM tiers usable
idea: Von Neumann's 1956 'probabilistic logics' built reliable organs from bundles of unreliable lines followed by a restoring majority stage. In stacked 3D DRAM, regions mapped as weak write each bit into vertically aligned cells on three different tiers and read them through a 3-input restoring sense stage, so one defective tier per column is harmless; a per-tier quality map keeps healthy regions in one-bit-per-cell mode.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): tier yield compounds over 26+ tiers; bundling tolerates per-tier defect rates near 1e-3 instead of 1e-7, so cheap tiers with weak lateral transistors become usable, paying 3x cells only where needed.

title: Eliminate per-company reliability qualification: national BEOL-memory test vehicle program
idea: Fund a shared public test chip and accelerated-aging method (drift, hydrogen, PBTI, disturb) for <=400 C memory devices, with open data and a JEDEC-track spec. Each startup then qualifies against a common model instead of spending 18-24 months on bespoke reliability work.
why: Qualification time and risk are the main barriers for new BEOL memory entrants; a shared vehicle could halve time-to-market and widen the supplier base.

title: Interference-litho array gratings with 6% spare bitlines
idea: TRIZ separation in space: the perfectly periodic array layers are patterned by mask-free laser interference lithography plus self-aligned multiple patterning on U.S.-built deposition/etch tools, leaving only relaxed-rule periphery for precision writing; stitch and standing-wave defects are absorbed by 6% spare bitlines and an ECC that knows defects arrive as whole columns.
why: Removes foreign scanners from array layers (5-7 EUV layers, fact 4) and cuts array patterning capital ~50%; reliability is bought with redundancy instead of tool perfection.

title: DDR5 on-die ECC miscorrection fixed by exposing syndromes to host
idea: DDR5's on-die SEC hides raw errors and can miscorrect a double error into a triple error that host Chipkill then misses. Fix: return the on-die syndrome bits in spare burst slots or a metadata sideband so the host decodes a true concatenated product code that knows which symbols the die already touched.
why: Restores end-to-end ECC strength so vendors can ship ~10x higher raw-BER cells (smaller Cs, relaxed tail screening, fact 1) at the same system FIT.

title: Neuroscientist's ion bath: printed ion-gel double-layer storage node
idea: Neurons hold state in ion gradients, not in dielectrics: the storage capacitor is replaced by a printed ion-gel electric-double-layer capacitor (~10 uF/cm2, about 100 fF/um2), so a planar 0.1 um2 node holds ~10 fF, twice a 70:1 pillar, and the charge margin is large enough that leaky, variable printed access transistors still meet retention.
why: Facts 1 and 2: the charge wall is broken without high-aspect-ratio etch, and the margin makes weak devices acceptable; the open question is whether ionic response in sub-100 nm films can reach ~10 ns.

title: Voyager concatenated coding across HBM dies forgives dry-bonded voids
idea: Voyager paired a convolutional inner code with a Reed-Solomon outer code so bursts the inner code missed were cleaned up. In HBM, each die keeps a light inner code while an outer Reed-Solomon code spans corresponding banks of all 12-16 dies (one symbol per die), so a die region lost to a bonding void or open TSV is just an erasure the outer code fills.
why: Water and HBM yield (fact 6): lets stacks use dry plasma-activated bonding and skip the CMP and post-CMP wet cleans that hybrid bonding needs (~10x less water in stacking) while recovering the 20-30% stack-yield loss; 6-12% outer-code overhead.

title: Three low-aspect capacitors vote as one via triple-row activation
idea: Reverse one strong cell into three weak ones: with fluorocarbon high-AR oxide etch banned, capacitors are built at ~20:1 in an amorphous-carbon mold patterned by O2 plasma (ZrO2 from amide ALD, TiN from TiCl4); each bit is written to 3 rows and read by activating all 3 at once, so charge sums on the bitline and one failed cell is outvoted.
why: Capacitor charge wall without PFAS etch: 3 x ~1.7 fF gives a 5 fF-class signal plus built-in single-cell fault tolerance; density cost is offset by far cheaper low-AR etch.

title: 4 ms cells allowed: compressed lines packed around weak bits
idea: Imposed limit: some cells may retain only 4 ms. Each 64 B line is compressed (base-delta or FPC), and the compressed payload is laid out so that the known weak bit positions in that physical line are skipped as don't-care holes. The weak-bit mask comes from a per-row fault map.
why: Rows with dozens of weak cells stay usable at normal refresh rates, so retention-tail binning loss (5-10% of rows) becomes near zero.

title: FeRAM imprint cancelled by scheduled whole-row polarity inversion
idea: Ferroelectric RAM (PZT, now HZO) fails by imprint: cells left in one state shift their coercive voltage until they will not switch or sense. Fix: a per-row inversion flag, so whenever a row is written its data is stored inverted with the flag toggled and every capacitor spends about half its life in each polarization, cancelling imprint.
why: Widens sense margin at high temperature, allowing thinner, lower-voltage HZO (voltage floor, fact 10) and longer retention.

title: Per-mat segmented back-bias wells tuned to measured leakage tail
idea: Effect: MOSFET body effect. The array p-well is split into per-mat wells isolated by deep n-well rings, each fed by a tiny local charge pump; mats with leakage tails get an extra -0.3 to -0.8 V reverse body bias (+60-100 mV Vt), while healthy mats stay at nominal bias and avoid the extra junction-field GIDL penalty.
why: Retention tail: ~5-10x leakage reduction on the worst mats without penalizing the whole die, so the refresh interval is set per mat, not by the die's worst cell.

title: Pastry chef's lamination: stack only known-good roll-to-roll memory foils
idea: Croissant dough is folded layer upon layer: 3D memory is built by laminating individually tested roll-to-roll memory foils (each a thin tier of printed or nanoimprinted cells), rejecting bad foil segments before lamination and joining tiers with laser-drilled, ink-filled vias, so stack yield no longer compounds as p^N.
why: Fact 2: monolithic 3D DRAM needs ~26+ tiers and its yield compounds per tier; known-good-tier lamination decouples yield from tier count.

title: Inkjet nanoparticle repair of interposer and module opens
idea: Display makers repair TFT line opens by direct printing; after test, inkjet silver or copper nanoparticle ink to bridge open RDL/interposer lines or rewire to spare channels, cured by low-temperature chemical (halide) sintering or IR diodes, avoiding xenon flash lamps and argon-carrier laser-CVD repair.
why: Rescues stacks and modules with a single open (fact 6), adding several points of assembled-HBM yield at no rare-gas cost.

title: Knitter's lifeline thread: epoch undo-log turns DUEs into rollbacks
idea: A knitter threads a lifeline so mistakes can be ripped back: the memory controller journals the old contents of overwritten lines for the last ~10 ms epoch into a protected region, so after an uncorrectable error the affected process or VM rolls back to the epoch boundary instead of crashing.
why: A DUE becomes recoverable, which lets designers use weaker ECC or longer refresh; a few percent bandwidth is the cost.

title: Tiny unbalanced sense amps with offsets mapped as erasures
idea: Po: the sense amp is allowed to guess. Sense amplifiers are shrunk to minimum-size devices with no offset cancellation; the ~1% whose static offset exceeds the bitline signal are found at test and their columns treated by the decoder as known-position erasures.
why: Periphery (fact 7): sense-amp stripe area down ~30-40%, total die area down ~6-10%.

title: Parametric charge pumping on common plate regenerates all cells continuously
idea: Effect: parametric amplification via a nonlinear C(V). Each storage node is a nonlinear MOS varactor plus a rectifying junction; a shared AC drive on the common plate pumps charge with a voltage-dependent sign, creating two stable fixed points, so every cell continuously restores itself toward its nearer rail with no row-by-row refresh. Reads compare node charge against a mid-level reference.
why: 10x density: cells tolerating ~1000x more leakage can be 2-terminal crosspoint varactor-diode stacks at 4F^2 in 8 BEOL layers (~10x); refresh counters, timers and restore-heavy sense periphery (fact 7) disappear, holding cost.

title: Water-hammer arrestor: transient deep-negative clamp on neighbour wordlines
idea: Plumbing arrestors absorb pressure spikes. While wordline i rises and falls, the sub-wordline drivers of i+-1 and i+-2 pulse deeper negative (about -0.5 V instead of -0.2 V), but only for the edge window. That damps capacitive coupling and electron injection into victims without the GIDL penalty that a constant deep negative bias would carry.
why: Could raise the hammer threshold 3-10x (fact 9) without counters, using only sub-wordline driver timing.

title: Hammer-proof zone of shield-row-separated pages for page tables
idea: Inverts 'every wordline must hold data': one cut mask converts every other wordline in 1/32 of each bank into a grounded shield row; the OS places page tables, kernel code and keys only in this zone, where no row has an active neighbor.
why: Eliminates the highest-impact row-hammer exploits (fact 9) for ~1.5% capacity, letting the rest of the die use cheaper probabilistic mitigation.

title: On-die micro-heaters anneal leaky access-transistor traps in the field
idea: Ideal: weak cells repair themselves. Closest: polysilicon heater lines under each mat drive local 250-350 C pulses lasting milliseconds (after migrating that mat's data) to anneal the interface and junction traps behind variable-retention-time and GIDL tail cells, resetting them to their low-leak state.
why: Fact 3: could shrink the leakage tail and VRT population 3-10x so refresh slows proportionally; also extends field life.

title: Coal-mine canaries: deliberately weak sentinel rows in every subarray
idea: Fabricate 2-4 canary rows per subarray with ~30% less capacitance, so they fail first as temperature, aging or hammer stress rises. The DRAM's internal logic samples them during standard REF slots. When canaries flip, it quietly spends extra internal refreshes on that subarray, the same way TRR already does, all within the unchanged DDR5/HBM REF protocol.
why: Replaces worst-case static guardbands with measured margin, so arrays can run close to their real retention and hammer limits: roughly 1.5-2x looser design margin for <0.1% area (facts 3, 9).

title: IBM RAIM moved inside the bank: parity rows rebuild hammered victims
idea: IBM's RAIM (RAID across memory channels) protects against whole-DIMM loss but never addressed row-level bursts such as hammer victims, which exceed per-line ECC. Fix: on-die logic maintains one XOR parity row per group of 32 rows in a subarray, updated on writes, so any single row corrupted beyond ECC is rebuilt from its siblings.
why: Converts row-hammer and single-row retention bursts into recoverable events, letting mitigation thresholds relax ~2-4x (fact 9) at ~3% capacity cost.

title: Buried electron-sink stripe between cells absorbs hammer carriers
idea: Po: rows have no neighbors. A shallow n-type collector stripe implanted between buried-wordline trenches and biased slightly positive captures electrons released by the aggressor's passing gate before they reach the victim storage-node junction.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) at the device level: claimed ~10x higher threshold; also trims junction-leakage coupling between adjacent cells.

title: Silicon nanocrystal electron-sink layer between wordlines stops hammer migration
idea: Scale jump (single migrating electron -> system security): row hammer is partly driven by electrons injected from the aggressor's passing gate that diffuse to the victim storage node. Embed a deep-trap Si/Ge nanocrystal layer in the inter-wordline isolation to capture and recombine them before they arrive.
why: Could raise the hammer threshold from ~1k toward ~10k+ activations, removing most mitigation refresh and bandwidth tax.

title: Eliminate in-DRAM parity: keep strong parity on flash, CRC in DRAM
idea: For read-mostly pages (weights, code, embeddings), DRAM stores only a 16-bit CRC per 512 B, and a strong Reed-Solomon parity block lives on CXL-attached flash or the SSD. A CRC miss triggers a parity fetch and reconstruction.
why: Frees most of the ~12.5% ECC overhead on the largest data class and tolerates weaker cells; ~10% more usable capacity at near-zero cost.

title: Second-life DRAM harvested from retired AI servers
idea: Rule: no retired DRAM goes to shredding. An industrial line desolders DRAM packages from 4-5-year-old hyperscaler boards, grades them with BIST, reballs them and assembles new modules with chipkill and stronger ECC for tier-2 CXL expansion memory, priced at 30-50% of new.
why: Adds supply equal to a fraction of annual fleet retirements at near-zero fab capex. Also raises U.S. manufacturability, because the work is assembly and test rather than wafer fabrication.

title: Ca: CaF2 crystalline gate insulator removes RTN traps from access devices
idea: Grow lattice-matched crystalline CaF2 on (111)-faceted recess sidewalls as the access-transistor gate insulator; a crystalline fluoride has far fewer border traps than amorphous SiO2/HfO2, eliminating the single-trap telegraph switching behind variable retention time.
why: VRT cells force multi-pass retention profiling and extra refresh margin (fact 3); removing them could cut VRT cells ~10x and simplify refresh binning.

title: LCD polarity inversion: per-row epoch flip of stored data
idea: LCDs invert pixel polarity every frame so that DC stress does not cause image sticking. Each row stores its data XORed with a per-row epoch bit that toggles on every scrub pass, so no cell or access transistor holds the same charge polarity for months. The controller decodes with the flag bit.
why: This balances BTI and data-pattern-dependent charge trapping, which drive aging and VRT, and it defeats hammer patterns tuned to particular data. It could shrink aging guardbands and data-dependent retention outliers by an estimated ~2x.

title: Ripstop quarantine bay: hot rows migrate into victimless sparse rows
idea: Ripstop fabric uses a reinforced grid where tears stop; reserve ~1% of each bank as a 'ripstop bay' in which only every third row holds data, and when the activation tracker flags an aggressor, migrate its data into the bay where it has no data-bearing physical neighbours to disturb.
why: Makes detected aggressors physically harmless instead of paying repeated victim refreshes (fact 9, ~1k ACT threshold); ~1-2% capacity versus up to 10-20% bandwidth for refresh-based mitigation.

title: Antivirus signature updates for fleet-learned hammer patterns
idea: Adapted from antivirus engines and immune memory, where a threat seen once anywhere becomes a signature everywhere: hyperscalers stream correctable-error locations and controller activation histograms to a central service that learns new hammer shapes (many-sided, half-double), compiles them into small finite-state detectors and pushes them fleet-wide as memory-controller microcode updates.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): mitigations frozen in silicon are bypassed within a year; patchable detection lets vendors ship lighter in-DRAM mitigation and keeps cheaper, more hammer-prone dies usable.

title: Air-traffic separation zones filled with checkable parity
idea: Adapted from air-traffic control, which keeps separation buffers between aircraft but watches them with radar: the OS page allocator places guard rows between security domains (ZebRAM-style), but instead of leaving them empty fills each with XOR parity of its neighboring data rows; guard rows are verified and rewritten at each scrub, so a hammer flip in a guard is detected and any flip in a data row is correctable.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): guard rows normally waste up to ~50% capacity; storing parity in them turns wasted space into correction capability on existing DRAM with software only.

title: JEDEC raw-BER memory class with mandatory host code
idea: Propose a JEDEC/OCP device class specified by raw bit-error rate (e.g., <=1e-6 per bit per second) instead of all-cell 64 ms retention. In exchange, the host must implement a defined end-to-end code and scrub rate.
why: Supply/yield/cost: lets fabs ship dies that fail the old retention screen and accept weaker cells, for a few % to 10%+ more bits per wafer.

title: HP/UCLA molecular crossbar's yield killer solved by defect-mapped stochastic decoders
idea: The 2007 160-kbit rotaxane molecular memory worked, but only ~25% of bits were usable and its decoders could not be lithographed at that pitch. Fix: adopt Teramac-style defect tolerance with nanowire decoders formed stochastically (random doping codes) and mapped at power-up, writing data only to verified bistable junctions through a logical-to-physical map with rateless coding across junctions.
why: Bistable molecular switches need no refresh; even accepting 75% defects at a few nm2 per bit could beat DRAM density by 10x or more.

title: Poisson-tail-derived scrubbing replaces 64 ms refresh
idea: Fit the measured retention distribution and compute the expected failures per 1 KB row at a 1 s interval (~0.5). Choose BCH t=6 per row so P(uncorrectable) < 1e-18, then replace blanket refresh with a read-correct-writeback scrub every 1 s.
why: Refresh (fact 3): ~15x less refresh energy and bandwidth, and tail cells become acceptable rather than repaired.

title: Alien coder's view: soft-decision LDPC fed by 3-bit sense amps
idea: An alien who sees DRAM only as a noisy channel would never throw away analog information: keep the latch sense amp but add 7 shared flash comparators per 8 columns that grade each bit's margin into log-likelihood ratios, and decode 512-byte pages with an on-die soft-decision LDPC that tolerates a raw BER of ~1e-3.
why: Fact 1 charge wall: cells with ~30% less capacitance (or a 4x longer refresh interval) become acceptable; soft decoding gains ~2 dB over hard SECDED.

title: Right-to-raw-errors mandate opens on-die ECC telemetry to hosts
idea: Worse: keep on-die ECC corrections hidden so hosts cannot see weakening rows until they fail. Flip: make CHIPS-funded purchases and JEDEC standards require DRAM to expose per-row corrected-error counters, retention bins and hammer counts through a standard health interface, so host software can do adaptive refresh, retirement and tiering.
why: Enables every other tolerance technique (adaptive refresh, elastic ECC, tiering) industry-wide so weaker cells can ship; a policy lever at near-zero cost.

title: Thin-oxide tunneling canary cells set each row's refresh interval
idea: Effect: direct/Fowler-Nordheim tunneling plus subthreshold leakage, made deliberately stronger. Each row carries 2-4 canary cells whose access device has a thinner gate oxide and shorter channel, so they fail ~4x earlier than the weakest real cell with the same temperature and voltage dependence. Rows refresh at a long default interval (256 ms+) and drop to a shorter interval only when a periodic check finds a flipped canary.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): ~99% of rows run 4x longer refresh, cutting refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and the 10-20% bandwidth tax ~3-4x; the canaries track temperature and aging automatically, so no profiling database is needed.

title: Minify waste: bin panel zones into gold, silver, bronze memory grades
idea: Panel uniformity is best at the center and worst near the edges. Test tiles by zone and package them as gold (servers), silver (PCs) and bronze (AI inference with host LDPC) grades instead of scrapping marginal regions.
why: Usable bits per panel rise ~10-20% with no process change; bronze grades monetize weaker cells.

title: Deuterium chimneys through the nitride over the array
idea: Inverts 'barrier layers must seal everything': the single added mask opens small windows in the hydrogen-blocking nitride over the array so a final deuterium anneal reaches storage-node junctions and gate interfaces, passivating dangling bonds with harder-to-break Si-D bonds.
why: Shrinks the trap-driven VRT and retention tail (fact 3) ~2-3x and hardens cells against hammer-induced trap generation; one non-EUV mask.

title: FeRAM's fab-poisoning PZT replaced by built-in-biased antiferroelectric ZrO2 capacitors
idea: Ramtron FeRAM never entered DRAM fabs because lead-based PZT contaminated lines and did not scale. Fix: use the ZrO2 that DRAM capacitors already deposit, an antiferroelectric, between asymmetric work-function electrodes (e.g., TiN bottom, high-work-function RuO2 top) whose built-in field shifts one double-hysteresis loop to zero bias, making the capacitor bistable and nonvolatile.
why: Zero refresh using existing DRAM dielectric and tools; antiferroelectric switching endures far more cycles than ferroelectric HZO, approaching DRAM-class endurance.

title: Substitute static twin-cell mode with on-the-fly pairing of weak rows
idea: Rows flagged weak by profiling switch into differential twin-cell mode (two adjacent cells per bit on complementary bitlines) under a mode bit, while healthy rows stay single-cell, so capacity loss is only local.
why: Retention tail: twin-cell mode gives ~4x retention margin to the worst ~1% of rows, letting the rest of the die run 4x slower refresh (fact 3).

title: T-RAM temperature failure fixed by replica-thyristor closed-loop gate biasing
idea: T-RAM stalled at GlobalFoundries because thyristor holding current swings by orders of magnitude from 0 to 105 C, losing data hot and writing slowly cold. Fix: every mat carries a replica thyristor whose holding current an on-die loop servos by adjusting the shared gate-assist voltage, keeping all cells a fixed margin above holding across temperature and aging.
why: Makes a capacitor-less one-device cell robust across corners, removing the capacitor wall and much sensing periphery (facts 1, 7).

title: Leak-direction-aware inversion: store each row mostly in safe state
idea: Combine data-bus inversion with the physics that true cells only leak 1->0: the controller inverts any row segment holding more charged than discharged cells and stores a flag bit, so at most half the cells sit in the vulnerable charged state; anti-cell regions use the opposite polarity.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): cuts the number of leakage-exposed cells ~30-50%, lowering retention errors and permitting longer refresh at ~1.5% overhead.

title: Substitute die scrap with elastic-capacity SKUs that shrink gracefully
idea: Swap the pass/fail bin for a 'degraded-capacity' product: dies failing retention or defect bins are sold at reduced capacity (e.g., 24 Gb from a 32 Gb die) with an exposed bad-region map that the OS/hypervisor offlines, sold to hyperscalers at a discount.
why: Supply strategy: recovers 5-15% of wafer output now scrapped or downbinned, a direct supply increase in a 4x-price market.

title: Quilt patches: per-row error-correcting pointers patch hot-emerging weak cells
idea: Each row carries a small on-die pointer field in a spare column (e.g. 4 pointers of address plus replacement bit); when 125 C scrubbing reveals a newly leaky cell, a pointer records it and the read path patches that bit independently of ECC.
why: Absorbs the weak population that grows over 10 years at 125 C without spending ECC strength, which stays reserved for random faults; ~1% overhead.

title: Si: mature-node hammer-guard buffer chip for commodity DIMMs
idea: A 10-person fabless team tapes out a small 28-40 nm companion chip on a multi-project wafer that sits beside the RCD, snoops ACT commands, keeps Misra-Gries hot-row counters and issues targeted refresh-management commands to any vendor's DRAM.
why: Retrofits strong row hammer protection (fact 9) onto cheaper DRAM using U.S.-manufacturable mature-node silicon.

title: Hermit-crab reuse mandate: thymus-screened retired DIMMs into CXL pools
idea: Hermit crabs live in shells others discard; a federal right-to-reuse rule plus procurement credit routes hyperscalers' decommissioned DDR4/DDR5 into CXL memory pools instead of shredders, after an automated 'thymic' stage that stress-tests each DIMM and maps out weak rows before reissue.
why: U.S. supply and cost per GB: retired server DRAM is sunk-cost capacity; reuse costs test plus CXL controller (~$0.05-0.1/GB), ~50-100x below new 2026 contract DRAM.

title: Harvested DDR4 into heavily coded CXL memory pools
idea: No EUV: put DDR4 from decommissioned servers behind CXL controllers that add chipkill-plus-erasure coding and per-row retirement, tolerating aged parts with higher error rates. Existing silicon becomes a second-life memory tier.
why: Adds already-made bits to supply with zero lithography; aged-part reliability is covered at the controller.

title: Eliminate separate ECC: lattice-coded multi-level charge across cell groups
idea: Write groups of 8 <=400 C oxide-TFT cells jointly as one point of a dense 8-D (E8) lattice of charge levels, as coded modulation does in modems. Decoding to the nearest lattice point corrects analog drift and noise directly, folding the error code into the multi-level storage.
why: ~2.5 bits per cell with a built-in ~3 dB coding gain, about 2x the density of SLC plus parity for BEOL cells with wide variation.

title: ML-grade memory class with declared raw BER
idea: Ideal: fabs build cells exactly as weak as the workload can tolerate. Closest: JEDEC/OCP define an ML-grade memory class that declares raw BER and retention distribution and mandates host-side strong ECC, so fabs can relax the capacitor target from ~5 fF to ~3 fF and ship parts that today fail retention screens.
why: Fact 1: relaxing Cs ~40% lowers pillar aspect ratio from ~70:1 toward ~45:1, cutting etch difficulty and yield loss while adding supply.

title: Eliminate retention binning on testers; characterize in the field instead
idea: Ship DRAM after only a short gross-defect test, skipping hours of ATE retention and burn-in screens. At every boot and in idle windows, an on-die BIST plus the controller maps weak rows, VRT cells and timing margins into a persistent profile stored in SPD/flash, and the system routes around them.
why: ATE time, burn-in and guard-bands are ~5-10% of DRAM cost; field profiling also recovers chips scrapped for marginal retention, adding several % sellable yield.

title: Mail carrier's redelivery: detect-only CRC for clean pages, refetch on error
idea: A mail carrier doesn't repair a damaged parcel but asks for another copy: pages with a clean backing copy (model weights, file cache, code) carry only a short CRC, and a detected error triggers a re-fetch from flash or a peer node; the parity bits saved go to capacity or to stronger codes for dirty pages.
why: ECC storage overhead falls from 12.5% to ~3% for read-mostly AI weights, so the same dies hold more weights.

title: Hot-stacked DRAM bonded straight onto accelerators at 115 C
idea: Po: memory that loves the heat. DRAM dies are hybrid-bonded directly onto accelerator logic with no thermal derating; at 105-125 C leakage rises roughly 8-30x, and refresh is set so the hot-spot raw BER stays at or below 1%, which the code corrects.
why: Data movement (fact 5): logic-on-DRAM stacking cuts movement energy from 3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit and removes the thermal objection to it.

title: Microwave kiln anneal heals implant damage in upper tiers
idea: Ceramic makers sinter in microwave kilns; activate dopants and heal implant damage in 3D tiers with 5.8 GHz microwave annealing at ~400-500C, replacing excimer melt-laser anneals (xenon/neon) and argon RTP, so end-of-range defects that cause junction leakage are repaired without cooking lower tiers.
why: Lower junction leakage tail in stacked tiers (facts 2, 3) at a rare-gas-free, low thermal budget; enables more tiers without retention loss.

title: Cryogenic DRAM revived where cooling already exists: 77 K no-refresh tier
idea: Cryogenic memory efforts (IBM's Josephson program, later cryo-DRAM studies) died on the cost of dedicated cooling. Fix: place a DRAM tier inside LN2 loops already present in immersion-cooled AI pods or HTS power distribution, where junction and subthreshold leakage collapse and retention stretches far beyond typical data lifetimes; refresh is disabled and data older than the qualified retention is poisoned and restored by software.
why: Zero refresh power plus lower wire resistance; the leakage tail (fact 3) effectively vanishes, allowing smaller capacitors (fact 1).

title: Just-enough-barrier volatile MRAM scrubbed every second
idea: Retention is tau = tau0*e^Delta, and write current scales with Delta. Nonvolatile MRAM over-pays at Delta ~60 kT. Size pMTJs for Delta ~38-40 kT: the per-cell flip probability is ~1e-8 per second, a 1 s ECC scrub catches the rare flips, and the smaller free layer packs denser.
why: Capacitorless, refresh-like scrub at 1 s. Write current -35%, write energy ~-50%, and lower barrier stress gives near-unlimited endurance.

title: Open-bitline twin-cell mode for hot and weak rows
idea: Inverts 'one bit, one cell, single-ended read': in open-bitline arrays the controller switches a row pair (row i in mat A and the mirror row in mat B, which share sense amps) into differential mode, writing true and complement and activating both, so the sense amp sees ~2x signal and common-mode disturbance (hammer, coupling, VARY noise) cancels.
why: Hammered or weak rows survive ~10x more activations and ~4x longer retention, costing half capacity only in those rows (<2% of the die).

title: Ba: barium-titanate acoustic sensors catch stack microcracks early
idea: Bond lead-free BaTiO3 piezo acoustic-emission sensors to HBM/3DS package lids; firmware listens for crack-burst signatures during thermal cycles and pre-emptively migrates data off the affected die and channel before joints open. Off-the-shelf piezo plus a small DSP board.
why: Converts sudden stack failures (fact 6) into planned remaps, cutting uncorrectable events and allowing cheaper, less-qualified stacks.

title: Garbage collector evacuates objects off error-rising rows
idea: Inverts 'errors are hidden from software': the controller exports per-row correctable-error counters to managed runtimes (JVM, Go, Python); their copying garbage collector, which already moves objects, preferentially evacuates live objects from rows with rising syndromes and marks those frames cold-only.
why: Zero-cost migration makes dies with growing faults (VRT, aging) usable; turns ~1% faulty rows into non-events instead of DIMM replacements.

title: Thrift store: refurbished hyperscaler DIMMs rehomed behind CXL ECC expanders
idea: Retired DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs are field-tested, binned and mounted on CXL expander cards whose controllers add symbol-level ECC, sparing and patrol scrub, giving them a second 3-5 year life as memory-tier capacity.
why: Adds GB supply with zero fab capex and zero new helium or quartz; the secondhand pool is hundreds of petabytes.

title: Context decoding: data-type priors resolve uncorrectable memory errors
idea: Readers fix typos from context. On a detected-uncorrectable error, the kernel lists the candidate codewords at minimum distance that fit the syndrome. It picks the one plausible for the data type: a pointer that is aligned and inside a valid VA range, a float exponent within the tensor's range, valid UTF-8, legal page-table bits. Type tags come from the compiler or the allocator, and the Linux patch plus evaluation fit within $1M.
why: Turning ~50-80% of DUEs into corrections allows cheaper ECC or relaxed refresh on weaker DRAM (facts 3 and 8).

title: Automotive remanufacturing: reclaimed server DRAM recertified with defect maps
idea: Adapted from remanufactured auto parts that are torn down, tested and resold with a warranty: retired DDR4/DDR5 RDIMMs from hyperscaler decommissions run through a retention-and-hammer characterization rack built from off-the-shelf FPGA testers, weak rows are written into an SPD-extension defect map, and modules ship with firmware that makes the OS retire those pages at boot.
why: Supply and scarce resources: at ~4x prices, a recertified channel adds bits with zero wafers, helium, quartz or EUV; recovering even 10% of decommissioned modules is a meaningful share of annual bit supply.

title: Cold-boot attacker insight: store each line in its discharge-safe polarity
idea: Cold-boot attackers know DRAM decays toward each cell's ground state. The host controller learns each row's true-cell or anti-cell polarity with a boot-time decay scan, then inverts each 64 B line so most cells hold the discharged state, which cannot leak away. One flag bit per line rides in spare ECC or metadata bits.
why: Real data is zero-heavy. Minimizing charged cells cuts retention and hammer error exposure by ~2-4x on the same silicon (facts 3, 9).

title: Letterpress fingerprint remap: nanoimprint template defects fixed once for all dies
idea: Worn letterpress type repeats the same blemish on every page; pattern critical array layers by nanoimprint cured with 365 nm UV-LEDs (no ArF/KrF excimers, which burn neon, argon and krypton), map the template's defects once, and burn one shared fuse remap into every die that template stamps, since its defects land at identical coordinates.
why: Removes neon-dependent litho and turns NIL's main weakness, repeating template defects, into a one-time characterisation instead of per-die yield loss; litho capex could fall by half (fact 4).

title: Murmuration checks: each cell group verifies seven neighbours in-array
idea: Starlings stay coherent by each tracking ~7 neighbours; place tiny check nodes in the CMOS under the array so each 8-cell group carries local parity shared with 7 overlapping neighbour groups (a spatially coupled LDPC evaluated locally), and the array iteratively corrects itself during refresh without shipping data to the controller.
why: Admits raw BER ~1e-3 media (orders of magnitude cheaper cells) at ~25% check overhead while keeping decode energy local; ~100x cheaper when paired with cheap-cell substrates.

title: Moore-Shannon quadded relays revived as stacked series access transistors
idea: Moore and Shannon (1956) built reliable switching networks from crummy relays by series-parallel quadding. Build each vertical-channel access device as two gate segments stacked along the same pillar and driven by one wordline; a cell leaks only if both segments carry tail defects (trap-assisted GIDL, junction traps), which squares the tail probability, and in 4F2 vertical cells the second gate costs height, not area.
why: Access-leakage tail (fact 3): tail fraction ~1e-5 to ~1e-10, so refresh is set by the bulk distribution (~1 s instead of 64 ms), saving most of the 16-33% idle refresh power; on-current falls ~2x, recovered with pillar height.

title: Elastic ECC migrates aging pages to stronger codes
idea: Worse: fix one ECC strength at manufacture, so the part over-protects when young and dies when old. Flip: the controller tracks corrected errors per page and promotes degrading pages to stronger codes (SEC-DED, then chipkill-class, then 2x replication) by borrowing capacity, so a module loses ~1% capacity per year instead of failing.
why: Lets makers ship weaker, cheaper cells with lighter guardbands, because end-of-life margin comes from adaptive overhead only where it is needed; ~2x module service life reduces new-bit demand.

title: Intel 1103 gain cells hold parity: physics diversity decorrelates failures
idea: Intel's 1970 1103 used a 3T cell read non-destructively through a gain transistor. Keep data in 1T1C cells but store the ECC check bits in a separate stripe of 3T gain cells, which have no capacitor, leak by a different mechanism and are not disturbed by wordline hammering, so one row event or leaky subarray cannot corrupt data and parity together.
why: Row hammer and retention tails (facts 3, 9): common-cause failures defeat ECC; diverse parity storage raises the effective correction of the same code, letting the data array run ~2x longer refresh with SECDED-sized overhead.

title: Mattress flipping: periodic true/complement inversion balances 10-year aging stress
idea: As mattresses are flipped to even wear, every few hours the controller rewrites each row inverted with a per-row polarity flag, so sense-amp pairs and capacitor dielectrics see balanced bias and BTI offset drift and polarity-dependent dielectric imprint stay symmetric at 125 C.
why: Ten years at 125 C can shift SA offset ~20-40 mV; balancing roughly halves drift, saving ~15% Cs margin or end-of-life refresh headroom.

title: Non-switching butterfly-capacitance read of ferroelectric cells
idea: Box [medium: HZO ferroelectric capacitor | access: planar | sense: small-signal capacitance at a fixed plate bias | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: ALD]. Instead of switching polarization to read it, the sense circuit applies a 50 mV probe at a fixed bias and measures differential capacitance, which differs between the two polarization branches of the butterfly C-V curve; the weak signal is decoded with soft ECC.
why: Constraint: no 2Pr switching charge moves on reads, ~10-30x lower read energy; reliability: removes read fatigue and wake-up wear, so endurance becomes effectively unlimited.
